title: The daily routine
teaches: Run the trading day on three checkpoints: a premarket that reads the futures, the calendar and the news, then narrows the list to a few names with levels, entries, stops and alerts; a midday check on what you hold, your stops and news due later; and a recap after the close that reviews stops, checks tonight's reports and writes tomorrow's plan.

walkthroughs.title: Before the open
steps: Run the day on three checkpoints: before the open, during the session, and after the close.
Start wide. Index futures trade nearly 24 hours, so they show how the market took the overnight news.
Then the calendar. CPI lands at 8:30 a.m. ET, and companies usually report before the open or after the close.
Then narrow your list to the few best names. Each gets levels, an entry, a stop and a risk amount.

walkthroughs.title: During the session
steps: Volume is usually heavy early, slows at midday, and picks up again into the close.
Midday is a check, not a hunt: what you own, your stops, and news due later, like a 2:00 p.m. Fed statement.
The rules you wrote stay the rules. Changes wait until the market is closed.

walkthroughs.title: After the close
steps: The recap starts with what you own. Check each stop, and consider raising it under a new higher low.
Check who reports tonight or before tomorrow's open. News after the close can gap a stock past your stop.
Then log today's ideas and write tomorrow's list and levels while the market is closed.
Veteran trader Gatis Roze found his best planned days generally gave his best results.

questions.q: Before the 9:30 a.m. ET open, what do S&P 500 futures show you?
choices: How the market takes overnight news
The exact price stocks will open at
Which stocks will lead the market today
Nothing that matters for stocks
questions.answer: How the market takes overnight news
questions.why: How the market takes overnight news. S&P 500 futures trade nearly 24 hours, so they react to off-hour news while the regular session is closed. SPY's premarket quotes move with them, and a big gap can move the largest index stocks too. They are a hint, not a promise. The open is set by supply and demand at the open, and premarket prices may not hold.
questions.lesson_line: Futures are the market's overnight vote. A hint about the open, not a promise.

wrong.The exact price stocks will open at: No. The open is set by supply and demand at the open itself, and premarket prices may not hold.
wrong.Nothing that matters for stocks: They do matter. SPY's premarket quotes move with the futures, and a big gap moves the largest index stocks too.
wrong.Which stocks will lead the market today: The futures track the whole index. They can't single out the names that will lead.

questions.simple: They show how the market is taking the overnight news, because index futures trade nearly all day and night.

questions.q: Midday is usually the busiest, most volatile stretch of the trading day.
questions.why: False. Midday is usually the calmest stretch, not the busiest. Volume is usually heavy early, often slows at midday and grows again near the close. The opening and closing hours tend to be the most volatile and active. Big news, like a Fed rate announcement, can upset that pattern on a given day.
questions.lesson_line: Busy open, quiet middle, busy close. Plan your checks around that shape.
questions.simple: False, because the middle of the day is usually the calmest stretch, and the busy times are the open and the close.

questions.q: You're building tomorrow's watchlist. What earns a stock a spot on it?
choices: It meets your setup criteria
It was today's biggest gainer
A chat room is buzzing about it
questions.why: It meets your setup criteria. A watchlist holds the names that fit your rules, so you can watch them for an entry signal.
questions.lesson_line: The list is for names that fit your setups, not names that are loud.

wrong.It was today's biggest gainer: A big day can be part of a setup, but on its own it's just a move. The list holds names that meet your criteria.
wrong.A chat room is buzzing about it: Buzz isn't a criterion. Investopedia warns that many chat-room posters have ulterior motives. Check the name against your own rules.

questions.q: Tap the word that fits the blank.
questions.sentence: The economic ___ lists the scheduled reports and events that can move the whole market.
questions.why: Calendar. The economic calendar lists the scheduled dates of big reports and events that can move a stock or the whole market. It covers reports such as jobless claims and interest rate announcements. BLS, for one, posts its release dates and times in Eastern Time.
questions.lesson_line: Check the economic calendar every premarket. A scheduled report can move the whole market.
questions.simple: Calendar, because the economic calendar is the list of dates when big reports and events come out.

questions.q: Your levels are marked on four names. How do you catch the moment one of them trades?
choices: Set price alerts at your levels
Keep flipping through the charts
Buy all four now so none get away
Check all four once, right at the open
questions.answer: Set price alerts at your levels
questions.why: Set price alerts at your levels. An alert pops up when a stock trades at a key price, so you know the moment a level trades. SMB trader Steve Spencer loads alerts at key prices before the open. Veteran trader Gatis Roze adjusts his alerts each morning. The alert tells you when to look. Your entry rules still decide whether to buy.
questions.lesson_line: Let alerts do the watching. You show up when a level trades.

wrong.Keep flipping through the charts: You'll catch some levels and miss others. An alert pops up the moment a stock trades at a key price.
wrong.Buy all four now so none get away: That skips your entry rules. Rules set before you buy are what take the guesswork out of the entry.
wrong.Check all four once, right at the open: A level can trade at any time in the session. An alert pops up whenever a stock trades at a key price.

questions.simple: Set price alerts at your levels, so the market tells you the moment one of them trades.

questions.q: Mid-session, the entry and stop rules you wrote before the open stay as they are.
questions.why: True. Write rules with clear signals that don't change while you're trading. Rework them when the market is closed. Don't change the plan as a knee-jerk reaction to a short-term move. Don't let impulse guide you during the session.
questions.lesson_line: During the session you execute. Rule changes wait for the close.
questions.simple: True, because your rules stay fixed while the market is open and only change after it closes.

questions.q: Your scan found a perfect-looking chart. What else does your premarket check before you plan the buy?
choices: The market's trend and its sector
Nothing, a great chart is enough
Analysts' price targets for it
How much buzz it has on social media
questions.answer: The market's trend and its sector
questions.why: The market's trend and its sector. Check the market's direction every day from the major averages, as CAN SLIM does. Short-term trades do better in the direction of the bigger trend. Leading stocks usually belong to leading industry groups or sectors. Veteran trader Gatis Roze finds a stock rarely rises apart from its sector. The chart still matters. It just isn't the whole check.
questions.lesson_line: Read the market and the group, then the stock.

wrong.Nothing, a great chart is enough: Charts don't trade in a vacuum. You do better trading in the direction of the bigger trend.
wrong.Analysts' price targets for it: A target is someone's opinion about where it could go. It doesn't tell you if the market is helping or hurting right now.
wrong.How much buzz it has on social media: Buzz isn't a criterion. Stock boards and chat rooms are full of people with their own motives.

questions.simple: Check the market's trend and the stock's sector, because trades do better with the trend and leaders usually sit in leading groups.

questions.story: CPI morning. The report is due at 8:30 a.m. ET. At 8:00 your plan is set: three names, with levels, entries and stops.
questions.q: How do you handle the report?
choices: Read the futures, then run the plan
Sit out the day until CPI is priced in
Scrap the plan and start over
Buy all three before it comes out
questions.answer: Read the futures, then run the plan
questions.why: Read the futures, then run the plan. Our rule: Fed and CPI days are traded like any other day. CME lists CPI among the economic reports that move markets. It lands at 8:30 a.m. ET, before stocks open at 9:30, so the futures react first. You read that reaction before the open, as on any morning. Then the plan's entries and stops do their job.
questions.lesson_line: Know the calendar, then read the futures and run the plan, as on any other day.

wrong.Scrap the plan and start over: Don't change a plan as a knee-jerk reaction to a short-term move. A CPI morning runs like any other.
wrong.Buy all three before it comes out: That bets on a number nobody has seen yet, in a thin premarket with little price competition. Our rules also allow no new buys outside regular trading hours.
wrong.Sit out the day until CPI is priced in: We have no news-day rule. Fed and CPI days are traded like any other day.

questions.simple: Read the futures, then run your plan, because our rule trades CPI days like any other day.

reasons: a release time (CPI 8:30 a.m. ET) that changes by date
rests on the owner's rulebook (C32, E58)

questions.q: S&P 500 futures were at 6,000 at 4:00 p.m. yesterday. At 8:45 a.m. today they're at 5,940. How far down are they, in percent?
questions.why: The drop is 6,000 minus 5,940, or 60 points. Divide it by the starting level of 6,000 to get 1%. Percent change is always measured from where you started, here yesterday's 4:00 p.m. level. One ES future tracks the 500 stocks, so the drop hints at a weaker open. SPY and the biggest index stocks tend to move with the futures, but premarket prices may not hold.
questions.lesson_line: Read futures in percent, not points. Points mean little until you size them against the level.
questions.simple: Down 1%, because the fall from 6,000 to 5,940 is one percent of where the futures started.

wrong.60%: Read the 60-point drop as 60%. Divide it by the starting level.
wrong.0.1%: A decimal slip: ten times too small.
wrong.10%: A decimal slip: ten times too big.

questions.q: Before the open you mark yesterday's open, high, low and close on a name. Which one is our default stop for a new long?
choices: Yesterday's low
Yesterday's high
Yesterday's close
Yesterday's open
questions.why: Yesterday's low. Our default stop is the low of the day or the prior day's low. It sits a few cents under that low, not exactly on it. Before the open, today's low doesn't exist yet, so yesterday's low is the one you can mark. The high and the close are worth marking too, but not as the stop.
questions.lesson_line: Mark yesterday's high and low on every name. Our default stop sits under a low.

wrong.Yesterday's high: Worth marking, but our default stop for a long sits under a low, not at a high.
wrong.Yesterday's close: Useful context, but our default stop uses the low of the day or the prior day's low, not the close.
wrong.Yesterday's open: Worth marking, but our default stop sits under a low: the day's low or the prior day's low.

questions.simple: Yesterday's low, because our default stop is the day's low or the prior day's low, and today's low doesn't exist yet.

reasons: key rests on one house fact (h1)
rests on the owner's rulebook (sizing_rule.md section 2 and F62)

questions.story: Sunday night your scans leave 45 names. Monday you get 20 minutes of prep before work.
questions.q: What do you do with the list tonight?
choices: Narrow it to the few best setups
Watch all 45 and react to movers
Buy a little of each to be safe
Add more names so you miss nothing
questions.answer: Narrow it to the few best setups
questions.why: Narrow it to the few best setups. Our rule: each day, a focus list of the 5 to 10 best setups, and the rest are ignored. Twenty minutes won't cover 45 charts well, so the narrowing happens tonight. Trading coach Brett Steenbarger notes that ranking ideas during prep is what lets you act fast when one sets up. A short list lets you watch the names that matter closely.
questions.lesson_line: Narrow your list. The best names get your attention, the rest wait.

wrong.Watch all 45 and react to movers: That's more than you can follow closely, and reacting to movers turns into chasing them.
wrong.Buy a little of each to be safe: That's dozens of trades with no plan behind any of them. Every buy needs an entry, a stop and a risk amount first.
wrong.Add more names so you miss nothing: More names means less attention on each one. Narrowing is what lets you act fast when one sets up.

questions.simple: Narrow it to the few best setups, because our rule is a focus list of the 5 to 10 best each day.

deeper.example: Sunday night, 45 names pass your scan. Rank them by how clean each setup is. Keep the best 5 to 10 and give each one levels, an entry, a stop, a size and an alert. Monday's 20 minutes then go to checking that short list against the futures and the news, not to finding it.

questions.story: Your plan: buy over $50, stop at $48, so $2 of risk a share. Overnight news hits, and the stock gaps up. At 9:45 a.m. it trades at $53.50.
questions.q: If you buy at $53.50, what's your risk per share to the $48 stop?
choices: $5.50, up from the planned $2
Still $2, the stop didn't move
$3.50, how far it gapped past $50
Less, the move is in my favor
questions.why: $5.50, up from the planned $2. Risk per share is entry minus stop: $53.50 minus $48. The stop stayed put, but the higher entry makes each share risk far more than the plan did. Our rule would skip this buy anyway. We never buy more than 4% above the buy point, and $53.50 is beyond that.
questions.lesson_line: A gap rewrites your plan's numbers. Never buy on the old math.

wrong.Still $2, the stop didn't move: The stop didn't move, but your entry did. Entry minus stop is now much wider.
wrong.$3.50, how far it gapped past $50: That's how far it ran past your $50 trigger, not the distance down to your stop.
wrong.Less, the move is in my favor: Paying more for the same stop means more risk per share, not less.

questions.simple: $5.50, because risk per share is your entry minus your stop, and $53.50 minus $48 is $5.50.

deeper.trap: The trap is the stop that didn't move. It feels like the plan still holds. But risk per share is entry minus stop, so at $53.50 each share risks $5.50, not $2. Buy the share count you planned for $2 of risk a share, and the trade risks far more than you meant.

reasons: story moved into the session in wave9 (E58)

questions.q: It's 12:30 p.m. and the market has gone quiet. What comes first in your midday check?
choices: Positions, stops and news due later
A fresh scan for new names to buy
Lower stops to give trades more room
Close it all out while it's quiet
questions.answer: Positions, stops and news due later
questions.why: Positions, stops and news due later. Veteran trader Gatis Roze checks what he owns first: protection takes precedence over fresh purchases. Each day, review open positions for new support and chances to adjust your stops. Know what's scheduled later too. Big news during the day, like a Fed rate announcement, can upset the usual rhythm. New buys can come later. They just don't come first.
questions.lesson_line: Midday is a check, not a hunt.

wrong.A fresh scan for new names to buy: New buys can wait. Veteran trader Gatis Roze checks what he owns first: protection takes precedence over fresh purchases.
wrong.Lower stops to give trades more room: Moving a stop lower on a long adds risk you never planned. Stops move with a trade, not away from it.
wrong.Close it all out while it's quiet: A quiet midday is normal: volume usually slows at midday and picks up near the close. Many day traders close up by then, but a swing trade runs on its plan and its stop.

questions.simple: Check what you own, your stops and news due later, because protecting your trades comes before hunting for new ones.

questions.story: At 2:00 p.m. the market whips both ways, and your stock swings through your stop and back. Later you learn the Fed's statement came out at 2:00.
questions.q: Which premarket step would have warned you?
choices: Checking the day's economic calendar
Reading the overnight index futures
Marking levels on each of your names
Scanning company news on your names
questions.why: Checking the day's economic calendar. It lists scheduled reports and events, including interest rate announcements. The Fed's Oct. 28, 2026 statement came out at 2:00 p.m. ET, in the middle of the session. Big news like that can upset the day's usual rhythm. The calendar tells you when to expect a jolt, not which way it goes. Our rule: Fed and CPI days are traded like any other day, so knowing the time just means no surprise.
questions.lesson_line: Levels tell you where. The calendar tells you when.

wrong.Reading the overnight index futures: Futures show the overnight mood. They don't tell you what's scheduled at 2:00 p.m.
wrong.Marking levels on each of your names: Levels tell you where to act, not when the market is about to jolt.
wrong.Scanning company news on your names: Company news matters, but a Fed statement is market-wide and scheduled. It sits on the economic calendar.

questions.simple: Checking the economic calendar, because it lists scheduled events like a Fed rate announcement that can jolt the whole market.

questions.story: After the close you run your recap. One holding just made a new higher low, well above your stop.
questions.q: What does the recap do with that stop?
choices: Consider raising it under that low
Consider lowering it for more room
Cancel it, since the trade is working
Raise it to today's closing price
questions.answer: Consider raising it under that low
questions.why: Consider raising it under that low. Each day, review open positions for new support levels and chances to adjust your stops. Support is usually a previous low, so a new higher low is the natural place to look. Our rule: the stop only moves up, never down or wider. Raising it is a judgment, not a must.
questions.lesson_line: Stops move one way: in the direction of the trade.

wrong.Cancel it, since the trade is working: Working trades can turn. Without a stop, a winner can become a loser.
wrong.Consider lowering it for more room: Our stop only moves up, never down or wider. Widening a stop on a winner adds risk for no reason.
wrong.Raise it to today's closing price: Support is usually a previous low, not a close. The new higher low is the level the trade should hold, so a raised stop goes under it.

questions.simple: Consider raising it to just under the new low, because a stop only moves up, in the direction of the trade.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (A4); may meet his trail rule E52 (owner flag)
key and one distractor reworded for balance

questions.story: You work 9 to 5 and can't watch the market. You hold two swing trades, each with a planned stop.
questions.q: Where should those stops live during the day?
choices: As stop orders at your broker
In your head, a lunch check
Nowhere until you get home
As alerts on your phone
questions.answer: As stop orders at your broker
questions.why: As stop orders at your broker. Our rule: every position has a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head. Stop orders can help protect against big declines, especially when you can't watch your positions. They are not a guarantee. A gap past your stop can cost more than you planned.
questions.lesson_line: If you can't watch, your stops have to be real orders, not intentions.

wrong.In your head, a lunch check: Between checks, nothing acts on it. Our rule is a real stop order with the broker, not a stop kept in your head.
wrong.Nowhere until you get home: Then a bad day has no limit until you're home. That's a loss you never planned.
wrong.As alerts on your phone: An alert only tells you a price traded. While you're at work and can't act, nothing sells.

questions.simple: As stop orders at your broker, because a real order acts on its own while you are at work and can't watch.

deeper.trap: The trap is thinking a stop order caps the loss exactly. It doesn't. If the stock gaps past your stop, the loss can be bigger than you planned, even with proper sizing. A real stop order still beats a stop in your head when you can't watch. Just size the trade knowing a gap can skip it.

questions.story: You skipped Monday's recap and Tuesday's prep. At 4:05 p.m. Tuesday, a stock you hold reports. It falls 11% after hours.
questions.q: What would have protected you from that 11% drop?
choices: Checking earnings dates for holdings
Reading the futures each morning
A tighter stop on that holding
The midday check on market volume
questions.why: Checking earnings dates for holdings. Companies usually report before the open or after the close. A weak report after the close can drop a stock fast in after-hours trading. Check the week ahead for earnings on what you own. Our rule: no new buys in the 3 days before a report. Hold through one only if the trade is up 5R. Knowing on Monday gave you Tuesday's session to act on that rule.
questions.lesson_line: Every day, check who reports tonight and tomorrow morning. Decide before the close, not after the gap.

wrong.Reading the futures each morning: Futures show the market's mood. They don't list a company's report date.
wrong.A tighter stop on that holding: A stop can't stop a report. The stock can gap past it, and the fill can land far below.
wrong.The midday check on market volume: Volume says nothing about a report date. The earnings calendar does.

questions.simple: Checking earnings dates for what you hold, because knowing the date lets you decide before the close, not after the gap.

deeper.trap: A tighter stop feels like protection here. It isn't. The report lands at 4:05 p.m., after the close, so the stock can open far below the stop the next morning. A gap past your stop can cost more than you planned. What works is knowing the date and applying our rule before the close.

questions.q: If you can't spend two hours on premarket prep, a routine isn't worth having.
questions.why: False. Veteran trader Gatis Roze says to design your routines around the time limits of your existing day. A good routine can pack a lot of information into a short window, as SMB trader Steve Spencer's does.
questions.lesson_line: Build the routine around the day you really have.
questions.simple: False, because a short routine built around the day you really have can still pack in a lot of information.

questions.story: For three weeks the S&P 500 has made lower highs and lower lows. Most names on your list broke support. One chart still looks perfect.
questions.q: How does your premarket treat that one name?
choices: Extra caution, the market is against it
Full size, it held when others broke
Buy the broken names, they're cheap
Short it, the market is falling
questions.answer: Extra caution, the market is against it
questions.why: Extra caution, the market is against it. Short-term trades do better in the direction of the bigger trend. Even strong growth stocks can drop fast when the market shifts. Our market reading guides it: Orange, only A+ setups; Red, mostly cash and shorts. Caution is not a ban. This one name has to clear a higher bar.
questions.lesson_line: Check the market before the stock. A great chart can still fail when the market falls.

wrong.Full size, it held when others broke: Holding up is not a free pass. Even strong growth stocks can drop fast when the market turns.
wrong.Buy the broken names, they're cheap: Broken support isn't a discount. It usually brings selling on the way back up.
wrong.Short it, the market is falling: Our shorts are the weakest stocks in the weakest groups. A chart that still looks perfect is the opposite of that.

questions.simple: Extra caution, because trades do better with the bigger trend, and even strong stocks can drop fast when the market turns.

deeper.trap: The trap is the one chart that holds up while everything around it breaks. It feels like strength, and sometimes it is. But even strong stocks can drop fast when the market turns. Broken support on the other names usually brings selling on the way back up. Treat the perfect chart as a name to watch closely, not a reason to ignore the market.

reasons: rests on the owner's rulebook (F65, C31)

questions.q: Written checklists are for beginners. Experienced traders run their routine from memory.
questions.why: False. Gatis Roze has traded his own account full time since 1989. He works from written checklists and says to keep them in sight. Out of sight is out of mind, he writes. A checklist tells him what's next and when the job is done. SMB's Steve Spencer keeps a set list for his morning.
questions.lesson_line: Out of sight is out of mind. Write the routine down and keep it where you can see it.
questions.simple: False, because a veteran trader who has traded since 1989 still works from written checklists kept in plain sight.

questions.story: Down day. You took two small losses, both by the plan, and still hold three names. It's 4:10 p.m., and you want to shut the laptop and forget it.
questions.q: What does tonight's recap still need?
choices: Stops, reports due, tomorrow's list
Nothing, a red day earns a break
A bigger list to win it back
Looser stops, so they don't hit
questions.why: Stops, reports due, tomorrow's list. The recap isn't a mood check. Review each open position and its stop, check the reports coming up, and write the next plan while the market is closed. Our rule adds one more step: journal every trade the same day, the two losses included. Trading more to win back a loss is revenge trading, and it backfires.
questions.lesson_line: Red day or green day, the recap runs. It's how tomorrow starts.

wrong.Nothing, a red day earns a break: Losses taken by the plan are the cost of trading. What you still hold and tomorrow's plan still need the recap.
wrong.A bigger list to win it back: That's trading more to win back a loss. Investopedia calls revenge trading a recipe for disaster.
wrong.Looser stops, so they don't hit: Our stop only moves up, never down or wider. A wider stop means a bigger loss when it's hit.

questions.simple: Review your stops, check who reports, and write tomorrow's list, because the recap sets up tomorrow whatever today felt like.

deeper.trap: The trap is the urge after a red day. Shutting the laptop skips the stops on the three names you still hold. Building a bigger list to win it back is revenge trading, which Investopedia calls a recipe for disaster. Widening stops breaks our rule: the stop only moves up. Two small losses taken by the plan mean the plan worked. The recap keeps it working.

questions.story: You work days. You get 20 minutes before work and about an hour after 5 p.m.
questions.q: Where does the heavy planning go?
choices: Evenings: list, levels, stops, size
Mornings: scan everything from scratch
Lunch break: scan and buy midday
Skip prep and react to the open
questions.why: Evenings: list, levels, stops, size. The hour after 5 p.m. is your longest window, and the market is closed. That is when the plan gets built. Our rule: every planned buy has its entry, stop and size written down before the market opens. The 20 morning minutes then go to the futures, the calendar and news on your names.
questions.lesson_line: Build the plan at night. Use the morning to check it, not to write it.

wrong.Mornings: scan everything from scratch: There's no time for that. Twenty minutes is for checking the plan, not building it.
wrong.Lunch break: scan and buy midday: Midday is for checking what you hold. Building the plan belongs to the hours when the market is closed.
wrong.Skip prep and react to the open: Then you decide on impulse, with no entry, stop or size written down before the open.

questions.simple: Evenings, because that is your longest window and the market is closed, so the short morning only checks the plan.

deeper.trap: The trap is the morning scan. Twenty minutes feels like prep time, but it can't build a list, levels and stops from scratch. Rushed, you end up reacting to the open, and the opening hour is one of the most volatile of the day. Build the list at night, and use the morning only to check it.

questions.story: After the close you run your recap. One holding is a fast mover, well above your stop and riding its rising averages.
questions.q: What does our trail rule have you do in the recap?
choices: Check for a close below the 10-day
Look for a close below the 21-day
Cancel the stop, it's working
Raise the stop to today's close
questions.answer: Check for a close below the 10-day
questions.why: Check for a close below the 10-day. Our default trail is the 10-day average for fast movers, the 21-day for steadier ones. We sell on a close below it, so the recap after the close is when you check. Each day, review open positions and chances to adjust your stops. Our stop only moves up, never down or wider.
questions.lesson_line: Stops move one way: up. Our trail is the rising average, checked after the close.
questions.simple: Check whether it closed below its 10-day average, because that is our default trail for a fast mover.

wrong.Look for a close below the 21-day: The 21-day is our trail for steadier names. For a fast mover, our default trail is the 10-day average.
wrong.Cancel the stop, it's working: The stop is the exit. Cancel it, and a working trade has no exit if it turns.
wrong.Raise the stop to today's close: Our default trail is an average, not the close. For a fast mover, that is the 10-day average.

reasons: re-keyed in wave9 to the owner's rulebook (E52, A4)

conflicts: Premarket start time: Investopedia (s13) says premarket trading runs from 4 a.m. ET; FINRA (s6) says it is 'typically defined as taking place from 7 - 9:30 a.m. ET'; brokers differ. The unit never keys a premarket start time (F1.05 owns session hours).

No single order for the premarket: Steenbarger (s40) starts with overseas markets, the day's economic reports, yesterday's indicators and overnight Globex; Roze (s35, s32) starts with the news, the Nasdaq premarket pages and overseas markets, then runs top-down (market trends, then sectors, then stocks); Spencer (s41) runs platforms, his game plan, alerts, a scanner and his journal. Investopedia's 10 Steps (s17) looks at the stock first and then steps back to the market, the reverse of Roze's top-down. So no question keys a fixed order of steps. The unit keys only what they share: plan when the market is closed (q06, q22), know the calendar (q04, q08, q14), narrow the list (q11), set levels, stops and alerts (q05, q10), and read the market as well as the stock (q07, q19). The row's 'P: order the routine' is taught that way.

Steenbarger (t2) modifies his game plan as the morning reports come out, while Investopedia (it1) and Fidelity (fp1) say the plan's rules should not change while you are trading. Not a contradiction: Steenbarger adjusts his read of the market; the entry and stop rules stay. q06 keys the rules; q08 keys adjusting the plan to the report.

Trading the open: Investopedia's beginner day-trading guide (s16) suggests novices watch the first 15-20 minutes, and Roze (s35) is 'seldom active' in the first hour, while Investopedia's timing piece (s14) says many professionals focus on the opening hour. The unit never keys whether to trade the open.

Mental vs hard stops: Roze (rf2) uses 'soft' (mental) stops because he watches all session. q16 keys only the case of a member who cannot watch (a resting stop order), with Schwab (sb5) and the gap caveat (ips2); it does not say mental stops are wrong for someone at the screen.

Roze's StockCharts articles date from 2012-2013. They are cited only for process advice that does not expire (write routines down, fit them to your day, plan when the market is closed, check the group). His lunchtime 'manipulation' view and the Trader's Almanac last-half-hour statistic in the same series are not used.

Investopedia's economic-calendar page (s19) suggests a trader who 'guesses correctly' can open a position right before an announcement. That is a gamble on an unseen number, and the unit teaches the opposite (q08 wrong choice 'Buy all three before it comes out'); only the page's definition of the calendar (ie1) is cited.

Futures hours: Investopedia's E-mini page gives Sunday-Friday 6 p.m. to 5 p.m. ET with a 5-6 p.m. halt, but CME's own contract-spec table loads by script and could not be read as page text. The unit says only 'nearly 24 hours' (CME's own product page, fc1) and never keys exact futures hours.

Unit plan row 'covers': course M6 'premarket routine' and dossier M12 are docs/curriculum, which the contract forbids as a source; not used. The Journal day-notes shape (prep, mid-day, recap) matches the unit's three checkpoints, but no house page states a routine in the owner's words, so the only house question (q10) rests on the owner's default stop (sizing_rule.md section 2), which F9.02 also asks directly; q10 asks it from the premarket angle (before the open only yesterday's low exists).

Overlap with F8.07 (the daily MENTAL routine, same Steenbarger morning posts): F8.07 owns the warm-up of the trader, breaks and the emotional cool-down; this unit owns the market and process side (futures, calendar, list, levels, alerts, midday check, the mechanical recap). Facts shared with F8.07 (Spencer's morning list, Steenbarger's game plan) are asked here from a different angle. Overlap with F7.07 (release times), F5.04 (earnings timing) and F1.05 / F10.04 (extended hours): those facts appear here only inside routine decisions, never asked as the same recall question.

Source check (checker, 2026-11-09): Investopedia's pre-market page (s13) now refuses every automated client (HTTP 402/403 to curl, the quote checker and WebFetch; the Wayback Machine's 2026 capture is also a 402). Its four quotes (ip1, ip2, ip3, ip5) were confirmed word for word on the Wayback Machine capture of 2025-08-21 (page 'Updated August 15, 2025', James Chen). The writer's 'updated 2026-09-17' could not be confirmed and was dropped from the title. They are evergreen market-structure facts; q01 and q09 also rest on CME's own page (fc1, fc5).
